answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. A collection letter violates the FDCPA if the least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read it to have two or more meanings, one of which is inaccurate.**

**A. The Act is read broadly and from the vantage of the least sophisticated debtor.**

The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) prohibits "any false, deceptive, or misleading representation or means in connection with the collection of any debt," including "[t]he use of any false representation or deceptive means to collect or attempt to collect any debt." 15 U.S.C. § 1692e, e(10). Because the statute is remedial, this Court construes its language broadly to effect its purpose. *Brown v. Card Serv. Ctr.*, 464 F.3d 450, 453 (3d Cir. 2006).

Courts therefore judge a collector's communication from the perspective of the least sophisticated debtor. *Id.* at 453–54; *Wilson v. Quadramed Corp.*, 225 F.3d 350, 354 (3d Cir. 2000). That standard is lower than the reasonable-debtor standard. *Brown*, 464 F.3d at 454; *Lesher v. Law Offices of Mitchell N. Kay, PC*, 650 F.3d 993, 997 (3d Cir. 2011). It protects the gullible along with the shrewd. The question is not whether a particular consumer was actually deceived, or whether a careful lawyer could arrive at the correct reading, but how the least sophisticated recipient could reasonably understand the letter.

**B. A reasonable but inaccurate second reading establishes deception.**

A debt collection letter "is deceptive when it can be reasonably read to have two or more different meanings, one of which is inaccurate." *Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354 (internal quotation marks omitted); *accord Brown*, 464 F.3d at 455. The rule does not require that the inaccurate meaning be the only one, or even the most natural one. A collector cannot escape liability by identifying an accurate interpretation if the letter also reasonably supports a false one.

This Court has applied these principles to language that misleads through implication. In *Brown*, a letter warning that nonpayment "could" result in referral to an attorney or a lawsuit stated a claim because it could deceive the least sophisticated debtor if the collector seldom took such action. 464 F.3d at 455–56. Literal possibility did not defeat the claim. In *Rosenau v. Unifund Corp.*, the Court reversed judgment on the pleadings where a letter from a collector's "Legal Department" could be read to suggest that an attorney was involved in collecting the debt. 539 F.3d 218, 223–24 (3d Cir. 2008). *Lesher* held that collection letters on law-firm letterhead misleadingly implied attorney involvement notwithstanding a disclaimer printed on the reverse. 650 F.3d at 1001–03. And in *Tatis v. Allied Interstate, LLC*, an offer to "settle" a time-barred debt stated a claim because the least sophisticated debtor could be misled into believing the debt was legally enforceable. 882 F.3d 422, 427–30 (3d Cir. 2018).

**C. The standard's limits do not excuse an objectively reasonable misreading.**

The standard does not impose liability for bizarre or idiosyncratic interpretations, and it presumes a basic level of understanding and a willingness to read the notice with care. *Campuzano-Burgos v. Midland Credit Mgmt., Inc.*, 550 F.3d 294, 298–99 (3d Cir. 2008); *see Wilson*, 225 F.3d at 354–55. Those limits screen out strained readings, not reasonable ones. A debtor who reads the entire letter carefully and still comes away with a reasonable but false understanding has not behaved idiosyncratically.

Nor is every technical inaccuracy actionable. A misstatement must be material, meaning capable of influencing the least sophisticated debtor's decision. *Jensen v. Pressler & Pressler*, 791 F.3d 413, 420–22 (3d Cir. 2015). A second meaning that misstates the debtor's rights, obligations, or consequences of nonpayment meets that test because it bears directly on whether, when, and how to pay or dispute the debt.

**D. Defendant's letter is deceptive.**

Defendant's letter states: "[quote operative language]." The least sophisticated debtor could reasonably read this language to mean [accurate meaning], but could just as reasonably read it to mean [inaccurate meaning]. The latter is false because [reason]. It is material because [effect on the debtor's decision]. The letter therefore violates 15 U.S.C. § 1692e, including § 1692e(10), and [the judgment should be reversed].
